notes:
1. Meaning of Citizenship

  • Citizenship is the legal membership of a person in a sovereign political community.

It creates a formal legal relationship between:

  • Individual.
  • State.
  • A citizen receives constitutional and legal protections.
  • A citizen also owes allegiance and civic obligations to the country.

In India, citizenship is governed mainly by:

  • Part II of the Constitution.
  • Citizenship Act, 1955.
  • Rules and orders made under that Act.
📌 Must-Memorise

Citizenship → Legal Membership of India

2. Citizenship and Nationality

  • The expressions citizenship and nationality are sometimes used interchangeably, particularly in international contexts.
  • In Indian constitutional law, citizenship generally refers to the legal status created by the Constitution and Citizenship Act.
  • Citizenship determines membership in India's political community.

3. Significance of Citizenship

Citizenship is important for matters such as:

  • Voting, subject to election law.
  • Contesting elections.
  • Holding specified constitutional offices.
  • Enjoyment of certain Fundamental Rights available only to citizens.
  • Obtaining an Indian passport, subject to law.
  • Full participation in the political community.

4. Citizens and Persons

The Constitution uses both the expressions:

  • Citizen.
  • Person.
  • Some constitutional rights are available only to citizens.
  • Several important rights are available to every person, including foreigners.
  • Citizenship therefore does not determine entitlement to every constitutional protection.

5. Citizenship Does Not Mean Immunity from Law

  • Citizenship does not exempt a person from criminal law.
  • It does not exempt a person from taxation.
  • Citizens remain subject to constitutional limitations.
  • Rights may be subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions.
  • Citizenship creates legal membership, not immunity from law.

6. Single Citizenship in India

  • India follows the principle of single citizenship.
  • A person is a citizen of India.
  • The Constitution does not create separate citizenship of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra or any other State.

India therefore combines:

  • Dual levels of government.
  • Single citizenship.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Single Citizenship

7. Purpose of Single Citizenship

Single citizenship promotes:

  • National unity.
  • Common political identity.
  • Equal civic membership.
  • Integration across State boundaries.
  • Freedom of movement and residence.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Federal Government Structure + Single Citizenship

8. Residence and Domicile Do Not Create State Citizenship

  • Single citizenship does not prevent valid residence-based requirements in specified fields.

Laws may use concepts such as:

  • Residence.
  • Domicile.
  • Local status.
  • These may be relevant to education, employment or welfare.
  • Such requirements do not create separate State citizenship.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

State Domicile ≠ State Citizenship

9. Part II — Citizenship

  • Part II of the Constitution is titled “Citizenship.”
  • It contains Articles 5 to 11.
  • These provisions primarily determined citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950.
  • They arose from the special historical circumstances of independence and Partition.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part II → Articles 5–11 → Citizenship

10. Article Mapping — Citizenship

  • Article 5 → Citizenship at commencement.
  • Article 6 → Migrants from Pakistan to India.
  • Article 7 → Persons who migrated to Pakistan.
  • Article 8 → Persons of Indian origin residing abroad.
  • Article 9 → Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.
  • Article 10 → Continuance of citizenship.
  • Article 11 → Parliament's power over citizenship.
🧠 Ultra-Short Memory

5 → Commencement
6 → Pakistan to India
7 → India to Pakistan
8 → Indian Origin Abroad
9 → Foreign Citizenship
10 → Continuance
11 → Parliament

11. Nature of Articles 5–10

  • Articles 5 to 10 were primarily commencement provisions.

They dealt with:

  • Partition.
  • Migration between India and Pakistan.
  • Indian-origin persons abroad.
  • Acquisition of foreign citizenship.
  • They were not intended to permanently regulate every future method of citizenship.

12. Article 11 — Continuing Parliamentary Power

Article 11 empowers Parliament to make laws concerning:

  • Acquisition of citizenship.
  • Termination of citizenship.
  • All other matters relating to citizenship.
  • Articles 5 to 10 do not limit Parliament's continuing legislative authority.
  • Parliament used this power to enact the Citizenship Act, 1955.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 11 → Parliament's Citizenship Power

13. Citizenship Is a Union Subject

  • Citizenship falls within the Union legislative sphere.
  • State Legislatures cannot independently create State citizenship.
  • Citizenship law is therefore principally made by Parliament.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

State Legislature → Cannot Create State Citizenship

14. Article 5 — Citizenship at Commencement

At commencement of the Constitution, a person could become an Indian citizen under Article 5 if:

  • The person had domicile in India, and

Satisfied at least one of the following:

  • Was born in the territory of India.
  • Either parent was born in the territory of India.
  • Had been ordinarily resident in India for at least five years immediately before commencement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 5 → Domicile + Birth/Parentage/5-Year Residence

15. Domicile under Article 5

  • Domicile was essential under Article 5.
  • Birth or residence alone was not sufficient.

Domicile broadly means:

  • Permanent legal home.
  • Intention to reside permanently or indefinitely.
  • Domicile is more enduring than temporary residence.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Article 5 → Domicile Essential

16. Article 5 Is Not the Present Birth Rule

  • Article 5 dealt with citizenship at commencement.
  • It is not the present general provision governing citizenship by birth.
  • Present citizenship by birth is primarily governed by Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 5 ≠ Present Citizenship-by-Birth Rule

17. Article 6 — Migrants from Pakistan to India

  • Article 6 dealt with persons who migrated to India from territory that became Pakistan.

It distinguished between migration:

  • Before 19 July 1948.
  • On or after 19 July 1948.
  • The date is important because of the migration permit system introduced during the Partition period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 6 → Pakistan to India
Key Date → 19 July 1948

18. Common Requirement under Article 6

  • The person, parent or grandparent had to have been born in India as defined under the historical Government of India Act, 1935 framework.
  • Article 6 therefore recognised both migration and Indian-origin connection.

19. Migration before 19 July 1948

  • A person migrating to India before 19 July 1948 could qualify if ordinarily resident in India since migration.
  • Formal registration under the later permit-based route was not required in the same manner.

20. Migration on or after 19 July 1948

A person migrating on or after 19 July 1948 generally required:

  • Registration as an Indian citizen.
  • Application before commencement of the Constitution.
  • Residence in India for at least six months immediately before the application.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Article 6 → Before vs After 19 July 1948

21. Article 7 — Migrants to Pakistan

  • Article 7 dealt with persons who migrated from India to Pakistan.
  • A person who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 was generally not treated as an Indian citizen under Articles 5 and 6.
  • Article 7 therefore dealt with the opposite direction of migration from Article 6.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 7 → India to Pakistan
Key Date → 1 March 1947

22. Exception under Article 7

A person who later returned to India under a permit for:

  • Resettlement.
  • Permanent return

could qualify under the special registration route connected with Article 6.

  • Article 7 therefore recognised a permanent-return exception.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 6 → Pakistan to India
Article 7 → India to Pakistan

23. Article 8 — Persons of Indian Origin Abroad

  • Article 8 dealt with certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India.
  • Eligibility required that the person, parent or grandparent had been born in India as historically defined.
  • The person had to ordinarily reside outside India.
  • Registration had to be made through an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 8 → Persons of Indian Origin Residing Abroad

24. Article 8 Registration

  • Registration could occur before or after commencement of the Constitution.
  • The purpose was to recognise constitutional citizenship links with members of the Indian-origin diaspora.

25. Article 8 vs OCI

Article 8:

  • Constitutional citizenship route.
  • Applied to specified persons at the commencement period.
  • Person became an Indian citizen.

OCI:

  • Statutory status.
  • Not full Indian citizenship.
  • Governed by the Citizenship Act and related rules.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 8 Citizenship ≠ OCI

26. Article 9 — Foreign Citizenship

  • Article 9 provides that a person cannot claim Indian citizenship under Articles 5, 6 or 8 if that person voluntarily acquired citizenship of a foreign State.
  • It reflects India's general approach against simultaneous full Indian citizenship and foreign citizenship.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 9 → Voluntary Foreign Citizenship

27. Article 10 — Continuance of Citizenship

  • Article 10 provides for continuance of citizenship of persons who were or were deemed Indian citizens under the preceding constitutional provisions.
  • Such continuance remains subject to any law made by Parliament.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 10 → Continuance of Citizenship

28. Article 9 vs Statutory Termination

Article 9:

  • Operates in relation to the commencement provisions.
  • Deals with voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.

Citizenship Act:

  • Provides continuing statutory rules on termination after commencement.

29. Citizenship Act, 1955

  • Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955 under Article 11.

It is the principal statute governing:

  • Acquisition of citizenship.
  • Termination of citizenship.
  • OCI cardholder registration.
  • Related citizenship matters.
  • The Act was enacted on 30 December 1955.
📌 Must-Memorise

Citizenship Act → 1955
Enacted → 30 December 1955

30. Five Modes of Acquisition

Indian citizenship may be acquired by:

1. Birth.

2. Descent.

3. Registration.

4. Naturalisation.

5. Incorporation of territory.

📌 Must-Memorise

Acquisition → Birth + Descent + Registration + Naturalisation + Incorporation

31. Three Modes of Loss

Indian citizenship may principally be lost by:

1. Renunciation.

2. Termination.

3. Deprivation.

📌 Must-Memorise

Loss → Renunciation + Termination + Deprivation

32. Important Citizenship Amendments

Major amendments to citizenship law include:

  • 1986.
  • 1992.
  • 2003.
  • 2005.
  • 2015.
  • 2019.

They affected matters such as:

  • Citizenship by birth.
  • Descent through mother.
  • Illegal migrants.
  • OCI.
  • Special citizenship provisions.

33. Citizenship by Birth — Section 3

Citizenship by birth depends on:

  • Date of birth.
  • Citizenship of parents.
  • Migration status of parents.
  • The statutory rules have changed over time.
📌 Must-Memorise

Citizenship by Birth → Section 3

34. Born from 26 January 1950 to before 1 July 1987

  • A person born in India during this period was generally an Indian citizen by birth.
  • Parental nationality was generally not decisive.

Exceptions applied to certain children of:

  • Foreign diplomats enjoying immunity.
  • Enemy aliens in territory under enemy occupation.
📌 Must-Memorise

26 Jan 1950–30 Jun 1987 → Birth in India Generally Sufficient

35. Born from 1 July 1987 to before 3 December 2004

  • A person born in India during this period became a citizen by birth if either parent was an Indian citizen at the time of birth.
📌 Must-Memorise

1 Jul 1987–2 Dec 2004 → One Parent Must Be Indian Citizen

36. Born on or after 3 December 2004

A person born in India qualifies by birth if:

  • Both parents are Indian citizens, or
  • One parent is an Indian citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant.
📌 Must-Memorise

From 3 Dec 2004 → Both Citizens OR One Citizen + Other Not Illegal Migrant

37. Birth in India Is Not Always Enough

  • For persons born on or after 3 December 2004, birthplace alone does not automatically establish citizenship.
  • Parentage and illegal-migrant status become relevant.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Born in India after 3 Dec 2004 → Citizenship Not Automatic Merely by Place of Birth

38. Citizenship-by-Birth Date Chain

  • 26 January 1950.
  • 1 July 1987.
  • 3 December 2004.
🧠 Ultra-Short Memory

1950 → Birth
1987 → One Parent
2004 → Parents + Illegal Migrant Condition

39. Citizenship by Descent — Section 4

  • Citizenship by descent principally applies to persons born outside India.
  • The applicable rule depends on the person's date of birth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Citizenship by Descent → Section 4

40. Born Outside India before 10 December 1992

  • A person could generally acquire citizenship by descent if the father was an Indian citizen at the time of birth.
  • The original system therefore followed a father-based rule.

41. Born from 10 December 1992 to before 3 December 2004

  • Citizenship by descent could arise if either parent was an Indian citizen.
  • The 1992 amendment removed the earlier father-only approach.
📌 Must-Memorise

1992 Amendment → Mother or Father Can Transmit Citizenship by Descent

42. Born Outside India on or after 3 December 2004

Citizenship by descent generally requires:

  • Either parent to be an Indian citizen.
  • Registration of birth at an Indian consulate within the prescribed period.
  • Required declaration relating to the child's foreign passport or nationality.

43. Birth vs Descent

Birth:

  • Person born in India.

Descent:

  • Person born outside India to Indian parent or parents, subject to statutory conditions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Section 3 → Birth
Section 4 → Descent

44. Citizenship by Registration — Section 5

  • Section 5 provides citizenship by registration.
  • The Central Government may register eligible applicants as Indian citizens.
  • Registration is available only to specified statutory categories.
  • It is not automatically available to every foreigner.
📌 Must-Memorise

Registration → Section 5

45. Important Registration Categories

Subject to statutory requirements, registration may be available to:

  • Person of Indian origin ordinarily resident in India.
  • Person of Indian origin ordinarily resident outside undivided India.
  • Person married to an Indian citizen and ordinarily resident in India.
  • Minor child of Indian citizens.
  • Person whose parents are registered Indian citizens.
  • Person who or whose parent was earlier a citizen of independent India.
  • Eligible OCI cardholder satisfying residence requirements.

46. Marriage Does Not Automatically Give Citizenship

  • A foreign spouse does not automatically become an Indian citizen by marrying an Indian citizen.

The spouse must:

  • Apply.
  • Meet statutory conditions.
  • Obtain registration approval.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Marriage to Indian Citizen ≠ Automatic Citizenship

47. Residence and Registration

  • Many registration categories require prescribed periods of ordinary residence or government service.
  • The Central Government must be satisfied that statutory conditions have been met.
  • Registration is therefore not automatic.

48. Oath of Allegiance

  • Adult applicants for citizenship by registration are generally required to take an oath of allegiance.
  • This expresses formal allegiance to India and its constitutional order.

49. Citizenship by Naturalisation — Section 6

  • A foreign national may apply for Indian citizenship by naturalisation under Section 6.
  • Naturalisation is subject to conditions contained mainly in the Third Schedule to the Citizenship Act.
📌 Must-Memorise

Naturalisation → Section 6

50. General Conditions for Naturalisation

The Third Schedule broadly considers matters such as:

  • Applicant not being a citizen of a country that prevents Indians from naturalising.
  • Renunciation of existing citizenship where required.
  • Prescribed residence or government service.
  • Good character.
  • Adequate knowledge of a language in the Eighth Schedule.
  • Intention to reside in India or serve specified Indian institutions.

51. General Residence Pattern for Naturalisation

The ordinary statutory rule broadly requires:

  • Twelve months' residence immediately before the application.
  • Eleven years' residence or qualifying government service during the preceding fourteen years.
  • This is commonly described as a twelve-year aggregate structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Naturalisation → 12 Months Immediately Before + 11 Years in Previous 14

52. Naturalisation and Eighth Schedule Language

  • An applicant is generally required to possess adequate knowledge of a language specified in the Eighth Schedule.
  • This is a frequently tested condition.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Naturalisation → Knowledge of Eighth Schedule Language

53. Waiver of Naturalisation Conditions

The Central Government may waive specified conditions when a person has rendered distinguished service to:

  • Science.
  • Philosophy.
  • Art.
  • Literature.
  • World peace.
  • Human progress.

54. Naturalisation Is Not a Fundamental Right

  • Satisfying residence conditions does not by itself create an absolute constitutional right to citizenship.
  • Grant of naturalisation remains governed by statute and administrative determination.

55. Citizenship by Incorporation of Territory — Section 7

  • Where a territory becomes part of India, the Central Government may specify by order which persons connected with that territory become Indian citizens.

The order may specify:

  • Eligible classes of persons.
  • Effective date.
  • Conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Incorporation of Territory → Section 7

56. Historical Relevance of Section 7

This route has relevance to territorial integration involving areas such as:

  • Goa, Daman and Diu.
  • Puducherry and associated territories.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
  • Sikkim under its distinct constitutional process.

57. Incorporation Is Not Ordinary Individual Naturalisation

Citizenship under incorporation of territory results from:

  • Territorial integration.
  • Central Government order.
  • Defined class of persons.
  • It is not merely an individual application route like registration or naturalisation.

58. Renunciation — Section 8

  • Renunciation is voluntary surrender of Indian citizenship.
  • An Indian citizen of full age and capacity may make a declaration renouncing citizenship.
  • The declaration becomes effective when registered by the prescribed authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

Renunciation → Section 8 → Voluntary Declaration

59. Effect on Minor Children

  • When a parent renounces Indian citizenship, the person's minor child may also cease to be an Indian citizen under the statutory rule.
  • Such a child may ordinarily resume citizenship within the prescribed period after attaining full age.

60. Renunciation during War

  • Registration of a renunciation declaration may be withheld when India is engaged in war.
  • This creates an important statutory exception.

61. Renunciation vs Termination

Renunciation:

  • Citizen makes formal voluntary declaration.

Termination:

  • Citizenship ends by operation of law following voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Renunciation ≠ Termination

62. Termination — Section 9

  • Indian citizenship terminates where an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country according to the Act.
  • India does not ordinarily permit full dual citizenship.
📌 Must-Memorise

Termination → Section 9 → Voluntary Foreign Citizenship

63. Determining Acquisition of Foreign Citizenship

Questions may arise concerning:

  • Whether foreign citizenship was acquired.
  • When it was acquired.
  • Whether the acquisition was voluntary.
  • These questions are determined under the statutory and procedural framework.

64. OCI Is Not Dual Citizenship

  • A former Indian citizen who later acquires foreign citizenship may qualify for OCI status if eligible.

OCI does not restore:

  • Full Indian citizenship.
  • Voting rights.
  • Eligibility for constitutional offices.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

OCI ≠ Dual Citizenship

65. Deprivation — Section 10

  • Deprivation is compulsory cancellation of citizenship by the Central Government.

It mainly applies to persons who acquired citizenship through:

  • Registration.
  • Naturalisation.
  • Certain incorporation-related routes.
  • It is not a general arbitrary power to remove citizenship from every citizen by birth.
📌 Must-Memorise

Deprivation → Section 10 → Compulsory Loss

66. Grounds for Deprivation

Citizenship may be deprived on grounds such as:

  • Fraud.
  • False representation.
  • Concealment of material facts.
  • Disloyalty or disaffection towards the Constitution.
  • Unlawful trading or communication with an enemy during war.
  • Specified imprisonment within five years after registration or naturalisation.
  • Continuous residence outside India for seven years, subject to statutory exceptions.

67. Public-Good Requirement

  • The Central Government must apply the statutory public-good test before deprivation where required.
  • Continuation of citizenship may be examined in relation to whether it is conducive to the public good.

68. Procedural Safeguards in Deprivation

The person ordinarily receives:

  • Notice.
  • Opportunity to seek inquiry.
  • Procedural consideration.
  • Deprivation is therefore a legal process, not an informal executive cancellation.

69. Deprivation vs Deportation

Deprivation:

  • Loss of citizenship.

Deportation:

  • Removal of a foreign national from India.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Deprivation ≠ Deportation

70. Meaning of Illegal Migrant

An illegal migrant broadly means a foreigner who:

  • Entered India without a valid passport or required travel documents, or
  • Entered lawfully but remained beyond the permitted period.

71. Effect of Illegal Migrant Status

Illegal migrants are generally excluded from ordinary routes such as:

  • Registration.
  • Naturalisation.
  • Exceptions may arise under statutory exemptions or special provisions.
  • Illegal-migrant status also affects citizenship by birth after 3 December 2004.

72. Illegal Migrant vs Foreigner

  • Every illegal migrant is a foreigner.
  • Every foreigner is not an illegal migrant.
  • A foreigner who remains in India under valid permission is lawfully present.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Illegal Migrant ⊂ Foreigner

73. Illegal Migrant vs Refugee

Illegal migrant:

  • Citizenship/immigration statutory category.

Refugee:

  • Person seeking protection from persecution or serious harm.
  • India does not have one comprehensive domestic refugee statute uniformly governing all refugees.
  • The concepts may overlap in some cases but are legally distinct.

74. Citizenship Amendment Act, 1986

  • The 1986 amendment restricted the earlier broad citizenship-by-birth rule.
  • For persons born from 1 July 1987, at least one parent had to be an Indian citizen.
📌 Must-Memorise

1986 Amendment → Restricted Citizenship by Birth

75. Citizenship Amendment Act, 1992

  • The 1992 amendment allowed citizenship by descent through either parent.
  • It removed the earlier father-only rule for the relevant period.
📌 Must-Memorise

1992 Amendment → Mother or Father

76. Citizenship Amendment Act, 2003

Major changes included:

  • Stricter citizenship-by-birth conditions.
  • Illegal-migrant provisions.
  • Framework for national registration.
  • OCI-related statutory development.
  • The stricter birth rule took effect from 3 December 2004.
📌 Must-Memorise

2003 Amendment → Stricter Birth Rule + Illegal Migrants + Registration Framework

77. Citizenship Amendment Act, 2005

  • The 2005 amendment expanded and modified provisions concerning OCI.
  • It formed an important stage in development of the overseas citizenship framework.

78. Citizenship Amendment Act, 2015

  • The 2015 amendment merged the earlier Person of Indian Origin card scheme into the OCI cardholder framework.
  • It consolidated overseas Indian-origin status under the OCI system.
📌 Must-Memorise

2015 → PIO + OCI Merger

79. Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019

  • The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 amended the Citizenship Act, 1955.
  • It created a special statutory acquisition route for specified persons from specified neighbouring countries.
  • It received assent in December 2019.
📌 Must-Memorise

CAA → 2019

80. Communities Covered by CAA, 2019

The specified communities are:

  • Hindu.
  • Sikh.
  • Buddhist.
  • Jain.
  • Parsi.
  • Christian.
🧠 Ultra-Short Memory

Hindu + Sikh + Buddhist + Jain + Parsi + Christian

81. Countries Covered by CAA, 2019

The specified countries are:

  • Afghanistan.
  • Bangladesh.
  • Pakistan.
📌 Must-Memorise

CAA Countries → Afghanistan + Bangladesh + Pakistan

82. CAA Cut-Off Date

The person must have entered India on or before:

  • 31 December 2014.
  • This date is central to the special statutory route.
📌 Must-Memorise

CAA Cut-Off → 31 December 2014

83. Effect of CAA Special Route

  • Specified persons meeting the conditions are not treated as illegal migrants for the relevant citizenship provisions.

They may apply for citizenship through:

  • Registration.
  • Naturalisation.
  • Citizenship is not automatic merely because a person belongs to a listed community.

84. Reduced Naturalisation Period under CAA

For the specified CAA category, the aggregate residence requirement under the Third Schedule was reduced from:

  • Eleven years.
  • To five years.
  • The immediately preceding twelve-month requirement remains relevant within the statutory framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

CAA → 11 Years Reduced to 5 Years for Specified Category

85. Areas Excluded from CAA Special Provisions

The special CAA provisions do not apply to:

Tribal areas under the Sixth Schedule in:

  • Assam.
  • Meghalaya.
  • Mizoram.
  • Tripura.
  • Areas covered by the Inner Line Permit system under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

CAA Exclusion → Sixth Schedule Areas + ILP Areas

86. CAA Does Not Automatically Grant Citizenship

An eligible applicant must:

  • Apply.
  • Produce prescribed documents.
  • Satisfy statutory conditions.
  • Receive approval.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CAA Eligibility ≠ Automatic Citizenship

87. CAA and Existing Indian Citizens

  • The special CAA provisions establish an acquisition route for specified applicants.
  • They do not contain a general provision cancelling citizenship of existing Indian citizens.

88. CAA vs NRC

CAA:

  • Amendment to citizenship-acquisition law.
  • Provides special route for specified applicants.

NRC:

  • Register intended to identify citizens under a separate legal and administrative framework.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CAA ≠ NRC

89. Citizenship Amendment Rules, 2024

  • The Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2024 were notified on 11 March 2024.
  • The Rules created procedures and forms for applications under the CAA framework.
  • They came into force upon publication.
📌 Must-Memorise

CAA Act → 2019
CAA Rules → 11 March 2024

90. Application Process under the 2024 Rules

The framework provides for:

  • Online application.
  • Document scrutiny.
  • Verification.
  • Oath of allegiance.
  • Consideration by designated committees.
  • Digital citizenship certificates where applicable.

91. District-Level and Empowered Committees

The 2024 Rules assign administrative functions to:

  • District-Level Committees.
  • Empowered Committees.
  • These bodies participate in verification and consideration of applications.

92. Documents under the CAA Rules

Applicants may need to provide material relating to:

  • Nationality or origin.
  • Entry into India.
  • Community.
  • Residence.
  • Eligibility.
  • Oath of allegiance.
  • The exact documentary requirements arise from the Rules and their schedules.

93. First Citizenship Certificates under 2024 Rules

  • The Ministry of Home Affairs announced the first set of citizenship certificates under the 2024 Rules in May 2024.
  • This is important as an implementation chronology fact.
📌 Must-Memorise

CAA Rules → March 2024
First Certificates → May 2024

94. Overseas Citizen of India — OCI

  • OCI is a special statutory status.
  • It is available to eligible persons of Indian origin and certain eligible family members.
  • OCI is governed by the Citizenship Act and related rules.
  • Despite the name, OCI is not full Indian citizenship.
📌 Must-Memorise

OCI → Statutory Status, Not Citizenship

95. OCI Is Not Dual Citizenship

An OCI cardholder is not:

  • Full Indian citizen.
  • Dual Indian citizen.
  • Holder of an Indian passport merely because of OCI status.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

OCI ≠ Dual Citizenship

96. Major OCI Benefits

Subject to applicable law and notifications, OCI cardholders generally receive benefits such as:

  • Multiple-entry lifelong visa.
  • Exemption from certain registration requirements for prolonged stay.
  • Parity with NRIs in specified economic, financial and educational fields.
  • Other notified facilities.

97. Major OCI Restrictions

OCI cardholders do not ordinarily possess:

  • Right to vote.
  • Right to contest elections.
  • Eligibility for President.
  • Eligibility for Vice-President.
  • Eligibility for Parliament.
  • Eligibility for State Legislature.
  • Eligibility for specified constitutional public offices.
  • General right to public employment.
  • Unrestricted right to acquire agricultural land.

98. OCI Registration and Cancellation

  • OCI status is obtained through application and registration by the Central Government.

OCI registration may be cancelled on statutory grounds such as:

  • Fraud.
  • Disaffection.
  • Security concerns.
  • Violation of specified laws.
  • Specified marriage-related circumstances in spouse-based cases.

99. PIO and OCI Merger

  • The earlier Person of Indian Origin card scheme was merged into the OCI framework in 2015.
  • PIO and OCI should therefore not be treated as two parallel current card systems under this framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

2015 → PIO Merged into OCI

100. Indian Citizen

An Indian citizen is a person possessing Indian citizenship under:

  • Constitution.
  • Citizenship Act.

A citizen may live:

  • In India.
  • Abroad.

101. Non-Resident Indian — NRI

  • An NRI is generally an Indian citizen residing outside India.
  • NRI is not a separate citizenship.

The exact definition of NRI may vary across:

  • Income-tax law.
  • Foreign-exchange law.
  • Other statutes.
📌 Must-Memorise

NRI → Indian Citizen Living Abroad

102. Foreigner

  • A foreigner is a person who is not an Indian citizen.

A foreigner may be:

  • Tourist.
  • Student.
  • Employee.
  • Diplomat.
  • Long-term resident.
  • OCI cardholder.

103. OCI Cardholder

  • An OCI cardholder is generally a foreign citizen with a special statutory connection to India.
  • OCI status does not create full Indian citizenship.
  • OCI cardholders normally use foreign passports.

104. Person of Indian Origin

  • “Person of Indian origin” is a descriptive and statutory expression used in various contexts.
  • A person of Indian origin is not automatically an Indian citizen.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian Origin ≠ Indian Citizenship

105. Citizen vs NRI vs OCI vs Foreigner

Indian Citizen:

  • Indian citizen → Yes.
  • Voting rights → Subject to election law.
  • Indian passport → Normally yes.

NRI:

  • Indian citizen → Yes.
  • Resides outside India.
  • Voting rights → Subject to electoral registration requirements.

OCI:

  • Indian citizen → No.
  • Foreign passport → Yes.
  • Voting rights → No.

Foreigner:

  • Indian citizen → No.
  • Voting rights → No.

106. Citizenship vs Domicile vs Residence

Citizenship:

  • National legal membership.

Domicile:

  • Permanent legal home.
  • Intention to remain permanently or indefinitely.

Residence:

  • Place where a person actually lives.
  • May be temporary, ordinary or long-term.
📌 Must-Memorise

Citizenship ≠ Domicile ≠ Residence

107. State Domicile

  • The Constitution does not create separate State citizenship.
  • The expression “State domicile” is commonly used in connection with residence or local-status requirements.
  • It does not mean separate citizenship of that State.

108. Citizen-Only Fundamental Rights

Important rights expressly associated with citizens include:

  • Article 15 → Protection against specified discrimination.
  • Article 16 → Equality of opportunity in public employment.
  • Article 19 → Six freedoms.
  • Article 29(1) → Protection of language, script and culture of sections of citizens.
📌 Must-Memorise

Citizen-Only → Articles 15, 16, 19, 29(1)

109. Rights Available to Persons

Important protections available to persons include:

  • Article 14.
  • Article 20.
  • Article 21.
  • Article 22.
  • These may extend to foreigners subject to constitutional exceptions.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Citizen vs Person Rights → Do Not Confuse

110. Citizenship and Voting

  • Only citizens may be registered as voters.

Voting also depends on:

  • Age.
  • Ordinary residence.
  • Electoral registration.
  • Absence of legal disqualification.
  • Citizenship alone does not automatically make every citizen an enrolled voter.

111. Constitutional Offices Requiring Citizenship

Indian citizenship is required for offices such as:

  • President.
  • Vice-President.
  • Governor.
  • Member of Parliament.
  • Member of State Legislature.
  • Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts, along with other qualifications.
  • Attorney-General.
  • Advocate-General through applicable qualification rules.

112. Citizenship and Public Employment

  • Article 16 protects equality of opportunity for citizens in public employment.

Eligibility for a particular post may additionally require:

  • Age.
  • Educational qualification.
  • Residence where constitutionally valid.
  • Other recruitment conditions.
  • Citizenship by itself is not sufficient for every public post.

113. State Trading Corporation v. CTO, 1963

  • The Supreme Court held that a company is not a citizen for the purpose of citizen-only Fundamental Rights such as Article 19.
  • Corporate personality therefore does not automatically create constitutional citizenship.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Trading Corporation Case, 1963 → Company Not Citizen under Article 19

114. Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India, 1962

The Supreme Court considered questions relating to:

  • Termination of citizenship.
  • Acquisition of foreign nationality.
  • Statutory determination of citizenship status.
  • The case is associated with Section 9-type termination issues.

115. Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India, 2005

  • The Supreme Court dealt with illegal migration and the legal framework applicable in Assam.
  • It struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983.
  • The case is important in the context of citizenship, migration and Assam.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sarbananda Sonowal → 2005 → Illegal Migration + Assam

116. Abdul Kuddus v. Union of India, 2019

  • The Supreme Court considered the legal character and consequences of Foreigners Tribunal decisions.
  • The case is relevant to citizenship determination and foreigners proceedings.

117. Current-Law Caution

Citizenship and immigration are governed through:

  • Acts.
  • Rules.
  • Notifications.
  • Tribunal procedures.
  • Judicial decisions.
  • Operational details may therefore change over time.
  • Recent administrative developments should be updated under Chapter 32 — Indian Polity Current Affairs rather than repeatedly rewriting the static constitutional chapter.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is citizenship? → Legal membership of a person in a sovereign political community.

Does India have single or dual citizenship? → Single citizenship.

Does India recognise separate State citizenship? → No.

Which Part deals with citizenship? → Part II.

Which Articles are in Part II? → Articles 5–11.

Which Article deals with citizenship at commencement? → Article 5.

What was essential under Article 5? → Domicile in India.

What additional conditions could satisfy Article 5? → Birth in India, birth of either parent in India, or five years' ordinary residence before commencement.

Is Article 5 the present citizenship-by-birth provision? → No.

Which Article deals with migrants from Pakistan to India? → Article 6.

What key date appears in Article 6? → 19 July 1948.

Which Article deals with migrants from India to Pakistan? → Article 7.

What key date appears in Article 7? → 1 March 1947.

Which Article deals with persons of Indian origin residing abroad? → Article 8.

Which Article deals with voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship? → Article 9.

Which Article deals with continuance of citizenship? → Article 10.

Which Article gives Parliament power over citizenship? → Article 11.

Which Act principally governs citizenship today? → Citizenship Act, 1955.

When was it enacted? → 30 December 1955.

What are the five modes of acquiring citizenship? → Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory.

What are the three principal modes of losing citizenship? → Renunciation, termination and deprivation.

Which Section deals with citizenship by birth? → Section 3.

Which Section deals with descent? → Section 4.

Which Section deals with registration? → Section 5.

Which Section deals with naturalisation? → Section 6.

Which Section deals with incorporation of territory? → Section 7.

Which Section deals with renunciation? → Section 8.

Which Section deals with termination? → Section 9.

Which Section deals with deprivation? → Section 10.

What was the general birth rule from 26 January 1950 to before 1 July 1987? → Birth in India generally conferred citizenship.

What changed from 1 July 1987? → At least one parent had to be an Indian citizen.

What changed from 3 December 2004? → Both parents must be Indian citizens, or one parent must be Indian and the other not an illegal migrant.

What are the three key citizenship-by-birth dates? → 26 January 1950, 1 July 1987 and 3 December 2004.

What was the descent rule before 10 December 1992? → Father generally had to be an Indian citizen.

What changed in 1992? → Either parent could transmit citizenship by descent.

What extra requirement applies for many births abroad after 3 December 2004? → Registration at an Indian consulate along with prescribed declarations.

Does marriage to an Indian citizen automatically confer citizenship? → No.

What is citizenship by registration? → Citizenship granted by the Central Government to specified statutory categories.

What is naturalisation? → Grant of citizenship to an eligible foreign national satisfying statutory conditions.

What language requirement applies to naturalisation? → Adequate knowledge of an Eighth Schedule language.

What is the general naturalisation residence pattern? → Twelve months immediately before application plus eleven years in the preceding fourteen years.

Can naturalisation conditions be waived? → Yes, in specified distinguished-service cases.

What is citizenship by incorporation of territory? → Citizenship granted to specified classes when territory becomes part of India.

What is renunciation? → Voluntary surrender of Indian citizenship.

What is termination? → Loss following voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.

What is deprivation? → Compulsory cancellation by the Central Government on statutory grounds.

Can minor children be affected by a parent's renunciation? → Yes, subject to statutory provisions.

Can citizenship be deprived for fraud? → Yes.

Can citizenship be deprived for specified disloyal conduct? → Yes.

What is an illegal migrant? → A foreigner entering without required documents or remaining beyond the authorised period.

Is every foreigner an illegal migrant? → No.

Is every illegal migrant a foreigner? → Yes.

Is a refugee legally identical to an illegal migrant? → No.

Which Amendment restricted citizenship by birth? → Citizenship Amendment Act, 1986.

Which Amendment allowed descent through the mother as well as father? → 1992 amendment.

Which Amendment introduced stricter birth and illegal-migrant provisions? → 2003 amendment.

Which amendment substantially developed OCI? → 2005 amendment.

Which amendment merged PIO and OCI? → 2015 amendment.

When was the Citizenship Amendment Act enacted? → 2019.

Which six communities are covered by the CAA special route? → Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian.

From which three countries? → Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

What is the CAA cut-off date? → 31 December 2014.

Did the CAA automatically grant citizenship to all eligible-category persons? → No.

What was reduced under the special CAA naturalisation route? → The aggregate residence requirement from eleven years to five years.

Which areas are excluded from the special CAA provisions? → Specified Sixth Schedule tribal areas and Inner Line Permit areas.

Is CAA the same as NRC? → No.

When were the Citizenship Amendment Rules notified? → 11 March 2024.

What administrative bodies appear under the 2024 Rules? → District-Level Committees and Empowered Committees.

When were the first citizenship certificates under the 2024 Rules announced? → May 2024.

What is OCI? → Overseas Citizen of India cardholder status under statute.

Is OCI full Indian citizenship? → No.

Is OCI dual citizenship? → No.

Does an OCI cardholder have voting rights? → No.

Can an OCI cardholder contest Indian elections? → No.

Can an OCI cardholder hold constitutional offices such as President? → No.

Which card scheme was merged with OCI in 2015? → PIO.

What is an NRI? → Generally an Indian citizen residing outside India.

Is an NRI still an Indian citizen? → Yes.

Is an OCI cardholder generally an Indian citizen? → No.

What is a foreigner? → A person who is not an Indian citizen.

What is domicile? → Permanent legal home with intention to remain permanently or indefinitely.

Is domicile the same as citizenship? → No.

Does “State domicile” create State citizenship? → No.

Which important Fundamental Rights are expressly citizen-only? → Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29(1).

Which major rights apply to persons generally? → Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22.

Does citizenship alone automatically give voting entitlement? → No; electoral registration and other legal conditions also apply.

Which case held that a company is not a citizen for Article 19? → State Trading Corporation v. CTO, 1963.

Which case is associated with termination following foreign nationality? → Izhar Ahmad Khan v. Union of India, 1962.

Which case struck down the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983? → Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India, 2005.

Which case dealt with Foreigners Tribunal decisions? → Abdul Kuddus v. Union of India, 2019.
